t: Valid Elements in an Array — Editorial
o: An element is valid if it is a strict prefix maximum (greater than everything to its left) or a strict suffix maximum (greater than everything to its right); the first and last elements are automatically valid. In Example 1, [1,2,4,2,3,2], the elements 1, 2, 4 each exceed all elements before them, and 3 exceeds all elements after it, while the middle 2s fail both tests. In Example 2, [5,5,5,5], strictness matters: no interior element is strictly greater than its neighbors' equal values, so only first and last survive. With n up to 100, even an O(n²) brute force checking every element against every other passes easily, but an O(n) prefix/suffix-max scan is the clean optimal solution.
k: Precompute suffix maximums so 'strictly greater than everything to the right' becomes one comparison per element.
Track a running left maximum in a single forward pass to test the prefix condition without nested loops.
Strictness means equal values never satisfy either condition — watch duplicates carefully.
First and last elements need no checks; they are always included.

a.i: For each index i, directly check whether nums[i] exceeds every element on its left or every element on its right using two inner loops. This mirrors the definition exactly and is trivially correct.
s: For each index i, assume validLeft = true and scan j < i: if any nums[j] >= nums[i], set validLeft = false.
Similarly compute validRight by scanning j > i for any nums[j] >= nums[i].
If validLeft or validRight, append nums[i] to the result.
a.t: O(n^2) — each element may be compared against all others.
a.sp: O(1) extra space besides the output list.

a.n: Approach 2: Prefix Max and Suffix Max (Optimal)
a.i: Precompute sufMax[i] = max of nums[i..n-1]. Then element i is valid iff it is strictly greater than preMax (max of everything to its left) or strictly greater than sufMax[i+1]. One backward pass builds suffix maxima and one forward pass with a running prefix maximum answers every query in O(1), giving O(n) total.
s: Build sufMax where sufMax[i] is the maximum of nums[i..n-1]; sufMax[n-1] = nums[n-1].
Initialize preMax = -infinity and an empty result list.
For each i from 0 to n-1: if preMax == -infinity or nums[i] > preMax or i == n-1 or nums[i] > sufMax[i+1], append nums[i].
a.t: O(n) — two linear passes over the array.
a.sp: O(n) for the suffix-maximum array (output excluded).

w: In an interview, mention the brute force briefly, then present the prefix/suffix-max solution as the intended O(n) answer. Common pitfalls: forgetting that comparisons must be *strict* (so duplicates like [5,5,5,5] yield only the endpoints), mishandling single-element arrays (answer is just [nums[0]]), and off-by-one errors at the boundaries — the first element has no left neighbors and the last has no right neighbors, so they always qualify. Edge cases to test: all-equal arrays, strictly increasing arrays (all elements valid via the left condition), strictly decreasing arrays (all valid via the right condition), and n = 1. A likely follow-up asks for O(1) extra space: you can compute validity in a second forward pass by first recording which indices beat the running prefix max, then doing a reverse pass tracking the right max — still O(n) time with only the output list as storage.
